title: Professional skills, Lesson 1: The one-page investment memo - conclusion first, evidence after
subtitle: The pyramid structure, falsifiable arguments, and writing for someone who reads three lines
whyItMatters: Good analysis presented badly does not exist. Decision-makers read ten memos a week and stop at the first three lines of each; if those three lines do not say what you recommend and why, nobody reads the analysis behind them.
openingQuestion: What should an investment memo open with?
openingOptions: The industry context and the history of the business being analysed
A specific recommendation with its three main reasons, in the first paragraph
The methodology and the data sources used through the analysis
A list of the main risks, so that the reader understands the limits of the analysis
explanation: This is the pyramid principle: conclusion first, argument second, data last. It runs opposite to how you were taught to write at school, where you lead gradually towards a conclusion. The reason is entirely practical: the reader of your memo is a decision-maker with ten minutes, not an examiner with an afternoon. If they agree after the first paragraph, the rest is there for them to check when needed. If they disagree, they know immediately where to push back.

realWorldExample.company: The memo on a chief investment officer's desk
realWorldExample.description: A typical CIO receives several memos a week from analysts. They almost all read them the same way: skim the opening for the recommendation, jump to the risk section to see whether the writer is self-aware, and only then return to the argument if it looks worth it. A memo that leads at length before reaching its conclusion is usually put down in the second paragraph - not because the analysis is poor but because the reader could not find what they came for.

sections.text: There is a rarely discussed gap between analysing something correctly and getting other people to act on your analysis. That gap is called presentation, and in financial analysis it has a fairly specific set of rules.
The four parts of a one-page memo

items: The recommendation: buy or sell, target price, time horizon - in two or three sentences
The argument: what the market is mispricing and why you think differently - the most valuable part
The evidence: two or three key facts and a summarised valuation
Risks and falsification criteria: what would have to happen for you to admit you were wrong

left.label: Description
left.text: The business has a strong brand, good margins and experienced management. All true, and the market knows it and has already paid for it.

right.label: An argument
right.text: The market is valuing the new division at zero because it is not yet profitable, while contribution margin turned positive last quarter and break-even is expected within four quarters.

sections.label: The severe test
sections.text: Reread your memo and ask: which sentence here could an intelligent person legitimately disagree with? If every sentence is an obvious truth nobody would contest, you have not made an argument - you have written a summary.
A falsifiable argument looks different from one that merely sounds good

left.label: Sounds good but cannot be tested
left.text: The business leads its industry, management is experienced, and there is large growth potential amid digital transformation. Nobody can argue with that sentence, and that is exactly the problem - a sentence nobody can argue with carries no information.

right.label: Can be tested
right.text: Gross margin will rise from 32% to 38% over the next 8 quarters, because the high-priced raw material contracts signed in 2023 expire next quarter and market prices are now 20% lower. That sentence can be wrong, and you will know when it is wrong - which is what makes it valuable.

sections.label: The severe test
sections.text: Reread the memo sentence by sentence and ask: is this a sentence an intelligent person reading the same data could legitimately disagree with. If every sentence draws a nod, you have made no recommendation - you are describing a business. A good memo always contains at least one sentence that makes the reader pause and think I am not sure that is right, because that is exactly where you are saying something the market has not priced in.

The pyramid structure has a very practical reason behind it: whoever receives the memo usually reads three lines and then decides whether to read on. So the recommendation has to sit on the first line, with the target price and horizon - not at the end as a conclusion arriving after the argument. That order runs against how we were taught to write, and against how you actually reached the conclusion. But a memo is not a record of your thinking; it is a tool for somebody else's decision.

lines: Writing clearly follows from thinking clearly; a tangled sentence almost always betrays an argument that is not finished.
The next lesson covers the harder part: defending that memo in front of an investment committee.

quiz.question: How does an investment argument differ from a description of a business?
options: An argument gives a fuller account of the history and business model
An argument states what the market is mispricing and why you think differently
An argument uses more quantitative data than an ordinary description
An argument is written at the end of the memo, once all the evidence has been laid out
quiz.explanation: Saying a business has a strong brand and good growth is not an argument, because the market knows that too and has paid for it. An argument has to answer: what do I see that the person selling me this share does not.

quiz.question: Why should the risk section not be written in general terms?
options: Because the risk section is the legal basis protecting the writer if the call is wrong
Because internal rules require every possible risk to the investment to be listed
Because readers use this section to judge how self-aware the writer is
Because generic risks make the memo run past the one-page limit
quiz.explanation: Writing that markets may be volatile says nothing at all. Writing that if gross margin falls below 18% this argument is wrong is a real risk: specific, testable, and it tells the reader what to watch.

quiz.question: How does the pyramid principle apply in a memo?
options: Start with the longest section and narrow gradually to the shortest at the end
Present the data first, the analysis second, and the conclusion at the very end
Split the memo into three equal parts by length to keep the content balanced
Conclusion at the top, the main arguments supporting it, detail underneath
quiz.explanation: This structure lets the reader stop at any level and still have the most important thing. It also forces the writer to know exactly what they are concluding - something many people only discover they do not, when they try to write the first sentence.

quiz.question: Why state explicitly what would prove you wrong?
options: Because it makes the argument testable and creates the discipline to exit
Because readers appreciate the modesty of the writer's reasoning
Because it is mandatory in every research report published to the market
Because it reduces the writer's responsibility if the call turns out badly
quiz.explanation: Without a falsification criterion, a wrong argument can be defended indefinitely by changing the reason - exactly the confirmation bias mechanism from the behavioural finance stage. Stating the failure condition in advance is the only way you will later be able to admit it.

quiz.question: Why should a memo state clearly what would prove the argument wrong?
options: Because the investment committee requires every memo to carry a full risk assessment
Because it turns the argument into something testable rather than a belief
Because it helps the writer avoid responsibility if the investment goes badly
Because this section replaces listing the risks
quiz.explanation: An argument that cannot say what would make it wrong cannot be wrong - and cannot be right in any useful way either. Writing it down in advance also helps you recognise when to exit, rather than reinterpreting every piece of bad news as neutral.

keyTakeaways: Conclusion first, argument second, data last - the reverse of how you were taught to write
The argument has to say what the market is missing, not merely describe the business
Risks must be specific and testable, with a clear numeric threshold
Always state in advance what would prove you wrong - that is discipline, not weakness

practicePrompt.question: Which opening sentence works best for a memo recommending a buy?
options: Business X is one of the leading players in Vietnamese retail
Recommend buying X, target price 35% higher, because the market values the new division at zero
This report analyses the outlook for business X over the next three years
Vietnamese retail is going through a period of change that is opening up many new opportunities
practicePrompt.explanation: Only this option contains all three components: a specific recommendation, the expected return, and an argument about what the market is missing. The other three are all true and carry no information - the reader still does not know what you want them to do.

application.title: The one-sentence test
application.message: Before writing anything, write one single sentence: what I recommend doing, and why. If you cannot write that sentence, you are not ready to write the memo - the problem is in the analysis rather than in the prose.
application.secondary: That sentence becomes the memo's first line, and usually the only line anyone remembers.

summary.keyIdea: The reader gives you three lines; spend them on the conclusion, not on context
summary.commonMistake: Leading at length before reaching the recommendation, so the reader gives up part-way
summary.action: Take an analysis you have done and rewrite it as one page in the pyramid structure.
